# `resource_policy`

The `resource_policy` block defines policies for infrastructure resources managed by Terraform. 

@include "beta.mdx"

## Configuration model

The `resource_policy` block supports the following configuration:

- `resource_policy` &nbsp "[`<resource_type>`](#resource-type)" &nbsp "[`<policy_label>`](#policy-label)" &nbsp block | repeatable
  - [`enforce`](#enforce) &nbsp block | repeatable
    - [`condition`](#condition) &nbsp boolean expression | required
    - [`error_message`](#error_message) &nbsp string | optional
    - [`info_message`](#info_message) &nbsp string | optional
  - [`enforcement_level`](#enforcement_level) &nbsp string | optional
  - [`filter`](#filter) &nbsp boolean expression | optional
  - [`locals`](#locals) &nbsp block | optional
    - `<name>` &nbsp any | repeatable
  - [`operations`](#operations) &nbsp list of strings | optional

## Complete configuration example

The following example demonstrates a `resource_policy` block with all configuration options specified:

<CodeBlockConfig filename="policies/example.policy.hcl">

```hcl
resource_policy "aws_instance" "testing" {
  operations        = ["create", "update"]
  enforcement_level = "mandatory"
  filter            = attrs.tags.env == "testing"
  
  locals {
    allowed_type = "t3.micro"
  }

  enforce {
    condition     = attrs.instance_type == local.allowed_type
    error_message = "Only ${local.allowed_type} instances are allowed in testing environments."
    info_message  = "Checking instance type: ${attrs.instance_type}"
  }
  
  enforce {
    condition     = attrs.monitoring == true
    error_message = "Monitoring must be enabled for all instances."
  }
}
```

</CodeBlockConfig>

## Specification

A `resource_policy` block supports the following configuration.

### Resource type

Specifies the resource type, such as `aws_instance`, `google_compute_instance`, or `azurerm_windows_virtual_machine`. You can use the `*` wildcard for all or part of the resource name to apply a policy to every resource defined in the configuration or every resource starting with a given prefix. Refer to the provider documentation for a list of supported resources for each provider.

### Policy label

Specifies a unique name for this policy within the policy file.

### `enforce`

The `enforce` block defines a condition that must evaluate to `true` for the policy to pass. You can declare more than one `enforce` block in each `resource_policy` block. If a condition in any `enforce` block fails during evaluation, then Terraform policy fails the entire policy and returns the corresponding error messages.

- Data type: Block
- Repeatable

An `enforce` block supports the following configuration.

#### `condition`

A boolean expression that must evaluate to `true` for the policy to pass.

- Data type: Boolean expression
- Required

#### `error_message`

The error message to display when the condition evaluates to `false`.

- Data type: String
- Default: None

#### `info_message`

An informational message to display regardless of whether the policy passes or fails.

- Data type: String
- Default: None

### `enforcement_level`

Specifies the enforcement level for the policy. You can specify one of the following values:

- `"advisory"`: Allows the operation to continue but prints a warning when the conditions of the policy aren't met.
- `"mandatory"`: Stops the operation if the conditions of the policy aren't met.
- `"mandatory_overridable"`: Stops the operation if the conditions of the policy aren't met, but allows a user with appropriate permissions to override the policy and continue.

- Data type: String
- Default: `"mandatory"`

### `filter`

Specifies a Boolean expression to filter which resources the policy applies to based on their attributes. Refer to [Attributes](#attributes) for information about how to access resource attributes.

- Data type: Boolean expression
- Default: None

### `locals`

Defines values that are local to the policy. You can only define one `locals` block per `resource_policy` block. The `locals` block nested in a `resource_policy` overrides `locals` blocks defined in the root of the policy file. Refer to the root-level [`locals` block reference](/terraform/policy/reference/policy/locals) for more information.

- Data type: Block
- Default: None

### `operations`

Specifies the Terraform operation during which to enforce this policy. You can configure the policy to evaluate during more than one operation. You can specify `"create"`, `"update"`, `"delete"`, or `"no-op"`.

- Data type: List of strings
- Default:
  - `["create", "update", "no-op"]` for policies that do not reference `prior_attrs`
  - None for policies that reference `prior_attrs`. You must set `operations` to `"update"`, `"delete"`, or both

#### The `attrs` and `prior_attrs` attributes

The `prior_attrs` attribute represents the state of the resource before the run. The `attrs` attribute represents the state of the resource after the run. Each operation determines which of these attributes are available.

| Operation | What the run does | `attrs` (after) | `prior_attrs` (before) |
|-----------|-------------------|-----------------|------------------------|
| `create` | Adds the resource | New values | Not available |
| `update` | Changes the resource | New values | Values before the change |
| `no-op` | Leaves the resource unchanged | Existing values | Not available |
| `delete` | Removes the resource | All null | Values before removal |

Operations fall into two groups, and for each resource policy, the `operations` list must stay within one group:

- **Operations with an "after" state**: `create`, `update`, and `no-op`. Refer to resource attributes with `attrs`. This is the default when you omit `operations`.
- **Operations with a "before" state**: `update` and `delete`. Refer to resource attributes with `prior_attrs`. You must set `operations` explicitly.

#### Choosing the right operations

The following table helps you select the appropriate `operations` configuration for common policy goals:

| Goal | `operations` | Resource attribute values |
|------|--------------|---------------|
| Ensure every resource meet the policy | Omit it or explitly set to `["create", "update", "no-op"]` | `attrs` |
| Ensure resources this run touches meet the policy | `["create", "update"]` | `attrs` |
| Block certain changes | `["update"]` | `attrs` and `prior_attrs` |
| Protect a resource from deletion | `["delete"]` | `prior_attrs` |

#### Operation constraints

The operation groupings create the following constraints:

- You cannot combine `delete` with `create` or `no-op`. A delete exposes only `prior_attrs`, while create and no-op expose only `attrs`. To evaluate both, split the policy into two separate `resource_policy` blocks.
- You cannot use `prior_attrs` with `create` or `no-op` operations because these operations have no prior state.
- Plans to replace resources are evaluated as two separate operations (delete and create), so you must implement policies that target both as two separate `resource_policy` blocks.

#### Default behavior

When you omit the `operations` attribute for policies that do not reference `prior_attrs`, Terraform policy defaults to evaluating `create`, `update`, and `no-op` operations.

To evaluate only changed resources and skip pre-existing unchanged resources, explicitly list the operations you want to evaluate, for example `operations = ["create", "update"]`.

An explicitly empty `operations = []` is unconstrained and evaluates all operations including `no-op` for policies that do not reference `prior_attrs`. Policies that reference `prior_attrs` cannot use `operations = []`. Terraform policy rejects it with the same error as a missing `operations` attribute.

#### Warning for incomplete coverage

When a policy calls `core::getresources` and its `operations` list leaves out `no-op`, Terraform policy loads the policy with a warning. Such a policy runs only for resources the current run changes, so a cross-resource check can miss pre-existing resources. Add `no-op` to the list, or keep the list as it is if you intend the policy to run only on changes.

Terraform policy does not warn for policies that reference `prior_attrs` or for lists that contain `delete`, because you cannot add `no-op` to either. It also does not detect `core::getresources` calls in file-level `locals`.

## Attributes

Within the `resource_policy` block, you have access to the following attributes.

| Object | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `attrs` | Provides access to the resource attributes after the run. |
| `prior_attrs` | Provides access to the resource attributes before the run. |
| `meta` | Provides access to Terraform-defined information about the resource. |

Refer to the [`operations`](#operations) section for details on how each operation determines which attributes are available.

Each Terraform provider defines the attributes available for each resource it supports. Refer to the provider documentation for a list of supported attributes.

### `meta` object attributes

The following meta-arguments are available in `resource_policy` blocks.

| Name | Description | Type | Example |
|------|-------------|------|---------|
| `meta.module_path` | The module path the resource belongs to. | String | `"."`, `"my-module"` |
| `meta.operation` | The operation being performed. | String | `"create"`, `"update"`, `"delete"`, `"no-op"` |
| `meta.provider_type` | The type of the provider of the resource. | String | `"aws"`, `"azurerm"` |
| `meta.tfe_stack.deployment_group` | The deployment group for Terraform Stacks. Empty string when evaluating workspaces. | String | `"us-east-1"`, `"global"` |
| `meta.tfe_stack.deployment_name` | The deployment name for Terraform Stacks. Empty string when evaluating workspaces. | String | `"production"`, `"staging"` |
| `meta.tfe_stack.stack_name` | The stack name for Terraform Stacks. Empty string when evaluating workspaces. | String | `"my-stack"`, `"infrastructure-stack"` |
| `meta.tfe_workspace.tags` | Tags for the current workspace. Empty map when evaluating Stacks or when the workspace has no tags. | Map(String) | `{"env" = "Production", "layer" = "Data"}` |
| `meta.type` | The type of the resource. This is the first label of the matching resource block. | String | `"aws_s3_bucket"`, `"azurerm_managed_disk"` |

## Examples

The following examples demonstrate common resource policy configuration patterns for specific use cases.

### Enforce instance type in testing environment

In the following example, the `resource_policy` block targets AWS instances in the testing environment and enforces that only t3.micro instances are allowed.

```hcl
resource_policy "aws_instance" "testing" {
  operations        = ["create", "update"]
  enforcement_level = "mandatory"
  filter            = attrs.tags.env == "testing"
  
  enforce {
    condition     = attrs.instance_type == "t3.micro"
    error_message = "Only t3.micro instances are allowed in testing environments."
  }
}
```

### Enforce encryption for EBS volumes

In the following example, the `resource_policy` block enforces that all EBS volumes must have encryption enabled.

```hcl
resource_policy "aws_ebs_volume" "encryption_required" {
  enforcement_level = "mandatory"

  enforce {
    condition     = attrs.encrypted == true
    error_message = "All EBS volumes must be encrypted."
  }
}
```

### Use wildcard to match multiple resource types

In the following example, the `resource_policy` block uses a wildcard pattern to apply a tagging requirement to all AWS resources.

```hcl
resource_policy "aws_*" "require_tags" {
  enforcement_level = "mandatory_overridable"

  enforce {
    condition     = attrs.tags != null && core::length(core::keys(attrs.tags)) > 0
    error_message = "All AWS resources must have at least one tag."
  }
}
```

### Enforce security group rules

In the following example, the `resource_policy` block uses a local value to check if a security group allows public ingress and enforces that it does not.

```hcl
resource_policy "aws_security_group" "no_public_ingress" {
  enforcement_level = "mandatory"

  locals {
    has_public_ingress = core::contains(
      [for rule in attrs.ingress : rule.cidr_blocks],
      ["0.0.0.0/0"]
    )
  }

  enforce {
    condition     = !local.has_public_ingress
    error_message = "Security groups must not allow ingress from 0.0.0.0/0."
  }
}
```

### Multiple enforce blocks

In the following example, the `resource_policy` block uses multiple `enforce` blocks to validate different security requirements for S3 buckets.

```hcl
resource_policy "aws_s3_bucket" "security_requirements" {
  enforcement_level = "mandatory"

  enforce {
    condition     = attrs.versioning[0].enabled == true
    error_message = "S3 bucket versioning must be enabled."
  }

  enforce {
    condition     = attrs.server_side_encryption_configuration != null
    error_message = "S3 bucket must have server-side encryption configured."
  }

  enforce {
    condition     = attrs.acl != "public-read" && attrs.acl != "public-read-write"
    error_message = "S3 bucket must not have public ACL."
  }
}
```

### Evaluate pre-existing resources with no-op

In the following example, the `resource_policy` block omits `operations`, so it defaults to `create`, `update`, and `no-op`. Terraform policy evaluates every CloudTrail in the workspace state, including trails that the current run does not change.

```hcl
resource_policy "aws_cloudtrail" "logging_enabled" {
  enforce {
    condition     = attrs.enable_logging == true
    error_message = "CloudTrail logging must be enabled."
  }
}
```
